 This Country Refunds Your Retirement Savings When You Leave. Working Holiday Visa Holders Pay 65% Tax.
 Home › Travel Insights › Money & Life Abroad This Country Refunds Your Retirement Savings When You Leave. Working Holiday Visa Holders Pay 65% Tax.
 Australia makes employers put 12% of pay into a retirement fund, and temporary workers can claim it after they go home. Most pay 35% tax on the payout. Working holiday visa holders pay 65%.
 By Rolando Herrera Last Updated Nov 15, 2026 8 min read Share Native Email Whatsapp Facebook X Linkedin In This Article The Money You Didn’t Know You Had Who Can Claim, and When The Two Tax Rates When You Switch Visas Why the Rate Is So High Don’t Leave It Behind Planning a Working Holiday Where In The World Australia; approximate city location Australia Australia Overview · Natural Earth In This Article

 The Money You Didn’t Know You Had Who Can Claim, and When The Two Tax Rates When You Switch Visas Why the Rate Is So High Don’t Leave It Behind Planning a Working Holiday Share Native Email Whatsapp Facebook X Linkedin Every paycheck in Australia comes with a second payment most foreign workers never see. By law, employers must add 12% of a worker’s ordinary earnings to a retirement fund called superannuation, or super. Australians can’t touch that money until retirement. Temporary visa holders can claim it as a lump sum once they leave the country and their visa ends.
 The refund comes with a large tax. The Australian Taxation Office’s rules for the departing payment withhold 35% of the main taxable part for most temporary visas. If any of the money was earned on a working holiday visa, subclass 417 or 462, the rate is 65% of the whole taxable amount. That second group includes young Americans, who travel on the 462.

 12% Of ordinary earnings that employers pay into super 35% Tax on most departing payouts 65% Tax if any of it was earned on a 417 or 462 visa 
 The Money You Didn’t Know You Had 
 Super is paid on top of wages, not taken out of them, so many short-term workers never notice it building up. The ATO confirmed that the rate employers must pay, called the super guarantee, rose to 12% on July 1, 2025. That was the last scheduled increase. Since July 2026, employers have had to pay it at the same time as wages rather than every quarter, so the balance now grows with each paycheck.
 A café job, a stint on a farm or a year in an office all count. If you held a temporary visa, earned wages and had a fund number on your payslip, there is probably money waiting. Some workers end up with more than one account because each employer opened a new one.
 The fund invests the balance and takes fees, and money paid into it is normally taxed at 15% on the way in. So the balance in your account is a little less than the 12% your employers contributed, before investment returns. That balance is what the departing payment draws on.
 The amounts add up faster than most people expect. A year of full-time hospitality work paying AUD 50,000 brings AUD 6,000 in employer contributions. Two years on a farm and in a café can easily leave a five-figure balance, spread across several funds.
 To see what you have, check your payslips for the fund name, look for the annual statement each fund sends, or link the ATO to a myGov account while you still have Australian contact details. The ATO’s online services list the super accounts held under your tax file number, including ones you have forgotten.
 Who Can Claim, and When 
 The ATO sets four conditions. You must have built up super while working on a temporary visa, not counting two retirement visa subclasses. The visa must have ended, by expiring or by cancellation. You must have left Australia and hold no other active Australian visa. And you can’t be an Australian citizen, a New Zealand citizen or a permanent resident.
 That last rule shapes the decision for anyone thinking of staying. Once you become a permanent resident, the departing payment is off the table, and the super stays locked until retirement age like any Australian’s. For many people that is the better outcome, because the money keeps growing without the exit tax. For someone who is leaving for good, the payment is the only way to get it out.
 Timing matters too. You can start an online application before you leave and finish it afterward. The ATO checks your visa status automatically with the Department of Home Affairs, so the claim can’t be paid until the visa has ended.
 The Two Tax Rates 
 The departing payment has a tax-free part and a taxable part. The tax-free part usually comes from personal after-tax contributions, which most short-term workers never make. Almost everything a temporary worker has in super is in the taxable part, which comes from employer contributions and earnings.
 For most temporary visas, including skilled work visas and student visas, the taxable part is taxed at 35%. For working holiday makers, it is taxed at 65%. The higher rate applies if any of the money was contributed while you held a 417 or 462 visa, or a bridging visa linked to one, so a working holiday followed by a skilled visa can still be caught.
 What a Year of Work Can Leave in Super Wages (AUD) Balance After 15% Entry Tax Payout at 35% Tax Payout at 65% Tax 
 30,000 3,060 1,989 1,071 
 50,000 5,100 3,315 1,785 
 70,000 7,140 4,641 2,499 
 The gap is large in dollars. A working holiday maker who earned AUD 50,000 might leave with about AUD 5,100 in super after the entry tax. At 35%, that would pay out about AUD 3,315. At 65%, it pays out about AUD 1,785, roughly $1,230 at recent exchange rates. Two people doing the same job for the same pay can receive very different amounts depending on the visa printed in their passport.
 When You Switch Visas 
 Many people arrive on a working holiday and stay on another visa, as a student, a sponsored worker or a partner. That path matters for the exit tax. The ATO applies the 65% rate to a payment if it includes any contributions made while you held a 417 or 462 visa, and the rate then covers the whole taxable part of that payment, not only the working holiday share.
 The ATO also says each super fund works out the rate for its own payment. So the visa history inside each account matters. A fund that only received contributions after you moved to a skilled or student visa would normally pay out at the ordinary 35% rate, while a fund that holds even a few months of working holiday contributions would pay out at 65%.
 That makes the usual advice to merge accounts more complicated for people who changed visas. Combining a working holiday account with a later account can bring the whole balance under the higher rate. Before you consolidate, ask each fund which visa periods its contributions cover, and get advice from a registered tax agent if the amounts are large.
 Why the Rate Is So High 
 The 65% rate came with Australia’s 2017 overhaul of taxes on working holiday makers, often called the backpacker tax, which also removed their tax-free threshold on wages. Super exists to fund retirement in Australia, and the exit tax reflects that: people who leave early can take the money out, but at a cost, and working holiday makers pay the most.
 The rule has drawn criticism over the years, but it remains in place, and the rates have not changed for the 2025 to 2026 year. For a traveler, the debate matters less than the arithmetic. The money is still yours, and 35 cents on the dollar is better than nothing.
 Don’t Leave It Behind 
 The biggest risk is not the tax. It is forgetting the money. If you don’t apply, your fund must transfer your balance to the ATO as unclaimed super once it has been six months or more since you left and your visa has ceased. You can still claim it from the ATO later, but every move makes the money harder to track, and some funds charge fees in the meantime.
 Before you fly home, collect the details you will need. Write down the name and member number of every super fund on your payslips. Ask your last employer to confirm that all the super you are owed has been paid. The ATO suggests preparing certified copies of your identification before you leave, because balances of AUD 5,000 or more may require them.
 Apply online. The ATO’s system is free to use and lets you claim from several funds in one application. Paper forms exist, one for super still held by a fund and one for super already transferred to the ATO, but online is faster. Be wary of companies that offer to claim your super for a fee. You can authorize a registered tax agent if you want help, but you don’t have to pay anyone to file a claim.
 Consolidate with care. Workers who held several jobs often have several small accounts, each charging fees, and combining them makes the final claim simpler. If every account dates from the same working holiday, merging costs nothing extra in tax. If you changed visas, read the section above first.
 Planning a Working Holiday 
 For Americans, the visa is the 462, called the Work and Holiday visa. According to Tourism Australia , it is open to people aged 18 to 30 with a passport from an eligible country, and the United States is on the list. It allows up to a year of travel and work, with extensions for people who complete regional work.
 Count the super as part of your pay, but at 35 cents on the dollar if you are on a working holiday. If you are budgeting for the trip, the refund can cover a flight home or the first weeks back. It won’t replace the 12% your employers paid in, and it is never sent automatically.
 Australia has more to sort out at the airport, too. Deep Arrival’s guide to claiming a GST refund before you drop your bag covers the shopping tax you can recover on departure. For a different way a country treats visitors and locals, see how Uruguay waives its hotel tax for guests who live abroad , and for a charge that lands on foreign residents instead, read about Dubai’s housing fee on the power bill .
 Eligibility, tax rates, unclaimed super rules and application steps are from the Australian Taxation Office. The super guarantee rate is from the ATO’s small business newsroom. Visa details are from Tourism Australia. All were read November 15, 2026. Worked examples are illustrations that ignore investment returns and fund fees. U.S. dollar estimates use about 69 U.S. cents per Australian dollar, the approximate rate on November 10, 2026. This is general information, not personal tax advice.
